title: Explaining how
job: Steps and instructions in order, and what they are for
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: -(eu)ryeomyeon IS THE INTENTION CLAUSE, and its main clause is an instruction or a requirement. haryeomyeon, garyeomyeon: if you mean to do it, if you mean to go. It is the ending a sign uses, and the only one of the two purpose frames that sits comfortably in front of an order.

-gi wihaeseo IS THE NEUTRAL PURPOSE ADVERBIAL, built on a nominalised stem: gagi, meokgi, hagi. It is heavier than -(eu)ryeomyeon and belongs in an explanation rather than a command — why you are doing a thing, said to someone who asked.

THE PURPOSE GOES IN FRONT, ALWAYS. English puts it last — press the button to open it — and Korean puts it first, so the whole sentence reverses. The literal line under every purpose sentence here shows the reversal rather than describing it.

ENGLISH try to MEANS ATTEMPT, POSSIBLY FAILING. -a/eo boda does not: it means do it and see how it goes. Hanbeon meogeoboseyo is an invitation, not a challenge, and translating try to with -a/eo boda teaches the wrong verb.

THE TRIAL AUXILIARY IS WRITTEN JOINED — haeboseyo, meogeoboseyo, nulleoboseyo, neoeoboseyo — following this course's -a/eo juda rows, which are all single tokens. Spaced, it would land on L2-M6's bwayo, a verb of seeing, and show a note that is false of the sentence.

THE SEQUENCING IS ALREADY BOUGHT AND IS ONLY REUSED. -go is L1-M3's, meonjeo, geu daeum-e and machimnae are L2-M10's. Nothing about ordering steps is reopened here; what is new is why a step is taken.
clause-(eu)myeon dwaeyo IS L3-M4's ENDING ON L2-M7's VERB, spent as permission rather than as condition: that is all you have to do. It answers is that it? and it costs this module no new key.

THE INSTRUCTION LINE IS L2-M1's -(eu)seyo AND NOTHING ELSE. No -(eu)psida and no -(eu)sipsio, which are L4-M7's; no written recipe style, which this course has nowhere; and no time clause, which is L4-M6's. Steps are ordered with adverbs and -go.

sentences.display: Meonjeo naembi-e mul-eul kkeurigo, geu daeum-e ramyeon-eul neoeuseyo.
sentences.script: 먼저 냄비에 물을 끓이고, 그 다음에 라면을 넣으세요.
sentences.cue: First boil water in the pot, then put the ramyeon in.
sentences.literal: first pot-in water-obj boil-and, that next-at ramyeon-obj put-please

words.note: The pan you boil in. It takes -e for what goes into it and -reul for the pot as a thing you use.
You boil something with this verb. The h is not heard: the romanization follows the sound, so the stem reads kkeuri- throughout.
The packet noodles, and the dish made from them. It is what a first set of Korean instructions is almost always about.
Put a thing inside another thing. The written h goes silent between vowels, so the endings read neoeu- and neoeo-.

words.cue: fire · a light · the heat under a pan
words.note: One word for the flame, the lamp and the burner. What English splits into light and heat, a kitchen instruction here keeps together.
Switches on a light, a screen or a burner. Its opposite is kkeoyo, and both take bul as their object in a kitchen.

sentences.trap: -go IS NOT and. It holds one instruction open until the next arrives, which is why the first step here has no -yo and no -seyo on it. Close it early and you have written two sentences with a comma between them.
sentences.sound: MEON-jeo NAEM-bi-e MU-reul kkeu-RI-go. Mul-eul runs together as MU-reul, and the h in kkeurigo is not pronounced at all.

variations.display: Meonjeo bul-eul kyeogo, geu daeum-e mul-eul kkeuriseyo.
variations.script: 먼저 불을 켜고, 그 다음에 물을 끓이세요.
variations.cue: First turn the heat on, then boil the water.
variations.changed: the stove step moved to the front, and the instruction ending on the boiling

variations.display: Meonjeo naembi-e mul-eul kkeurigo, geu daeum-e sogeum-eul neoeuseyo.
variations.script: 먼저 냄비에 물을 끓이고, 그 다음에 소금을 넣으세요.
variations.cue: First boil water in the pot, then add the salt.
variations.changed: salt in place of the noodles, on the same two-step frame

mistake.display: Meonjeo naembi-e mul-eul kkeuriseyo, geu daeum-e ramyeon-eul neoeuseyo.
mistake.script: 먼저 냄비에 물을 끓이세요, 그 다음에 라면을 넣으세요.
mistake.why: Two finished instructions with a comma between them are two sentences. One instruction in two steps takes -go on the first.

sentences.usage: Talking someone through a packet of noodles, at the stove or over the phone.
sentences.mnemonic: -go holds the step open, -seyo closes it.

sentences.display: Meonjeo sunseo-reul bogo, geu daeum-e beoteun-eul nureuseyo.
sentences.script: 먼저 순서를 보고, 그 다음에 버튼을 누르세요.
sentences.cue: First look at the order of steps, then press the button.
sentences.literal: first order-obj look-and, that next-at button-obj press-please

words.note: The sequence itself. With -daero it becomes in that order, which is how a machine or a recipe tells you to follow it.
The -go and -seyo shapes of L2-M6's bwayo, which is the row that owns the verb. Same word, different endings.
The button on a machine, borrowed straight from English. A shirt button is also beoteun.
Press or hold down. The stem doubles its l before a vowel ending, so the plain present is nulleoyo, not nureoyo.
The display surface of a machine — a ticket kiosk, a phone, a television. Not the device, only the face of it.

sentences.trap: bogo AND boseyo ARE THE SAME VERB AS L2-M6's bwayo. English changes nothing between I see it and look at it; Korean changes the ending, and the ending is what says whether you are reporting or instructing.
sentences.sound: MEON-jeo SUN-seo-reul BO-go. Nureuseyo is nu-REU-se-yo, three light syllables before the ending.

variations.display: Meonjeo hwamyeon-eul bogo, geu daeum-e beoteun-eul nureuseyo.
variations.script: 먼저 화면을 보고, 그 다음에 버튼을 누르세요.
variations.cue: First look at the screen, then press the button.
variations.changed: what you look at: the screen rather than the list of steps

variations.cue: First look at the order of steps.
variations.changed: one step standing alone, so the ending closes it

mistake.display: Meonjeo sunseo-reul bwayo, geu daeum-e beoteun-eul nureuseyo.
mistake.script: 먼저 순서를 봐요, 그 다음에 버튼을 누르세요.
mistake.why: bwayo reports what someone sees. A step that continues into the next takes bogo, and a step told to a person takes boseyo.

sentences.usage: At a ticket machine or a kiosk, walking someone through the screen.

sentences.cue: If you want to go to the station, go this way.

words.note: L1-M2's gada with -(eu)ryeomyeon on it. It states an intention, and what follows is what you must do about it.

sentences.trap: THE INTENTION COMES FIRST. English says go this way to get to the station and puts the purpose last. Korean has no order in which garyeomyeon could follow gaseyo, so the whole sentence reverses.
sentences.sound: YEO-ge ga-RYEO-myeon. Yeok-e runs together as YEO-ge, and i-jjok-euro is i-JJO-geu-ro.

variations.cue: If you want to go to the station, press this.
variations.changed: the instruction: a machine rather than a direction

variations.cue: If you want to make a booking, go this way.
variations.changed: the intention: booking rather than travelling

mistake.why: -gi wihaeseo explains a purpose to someone who asked. In front of an order it sits heavily; an instruction takes -(eu)ryeomyeon.

sentences.usage: Answering someone lost in a station or a shopping centre.
sentences.mnemonic: -ryeomyeon asks what you want, then tells you.

sentences.cue: If you want to make a booking, press this.

words.note: A reservation of any kind — a table, a seat, an appointment. It pairs with hada, so the verb is yeyak-eul haeyo.
L1-M4's hada with -(eu)ryeomyeon on it. It is the shape a sign uses above a machine or beside a form.

sentences.trap: haryeomyeon IS NOT hamyeon. L3-M4's hamyeon says if you do it; haryeomyeon says if you want to do it. The intention is inside the ending, and English has to add a whole verb to carry it.
sentences.sound: ye-YA-geul ha-RYEO-myeon. Yeyak-eul runs together as ye-YA-geul.

variations.cue: If you want to make a booking, look at the screen.
variations.changed: the screen instead of the button

variations.cue: If you want to make ramyeon, boil water.
variations.changed: a kitchen rather than a machine

mistake.why: nulleoyo says what somebody does. Telling a person to do it takes nureuseyo, which is what a sign or a helper says.

sentences.usage: Reading a kiosk out loud for someone who cannot see the screen.
sentences.mnemonic: haryeomyeon is the sign, hamyeon is the condition.

words.note: One word, not a count. Written together it means give it a go rather than exactly one time, and it is what softens an invitation.
L1-M3's meokda with the trial auxiliary joined onto it. Eat it and see what you think — an offer, and never a dare.

sentences.trap: THIS IS NOT try to eat it. English try to means attempt, and possibly fail. -a/eo boda means do it and see how it goes, so meogeoboseyo hands the food over rather than doubting the person can manage it.
sentences.sound: ra-MYEO-neul HAN-beon meo-geo-BO-se-yo. The auxiliary carries no break: it is one long word.

variations.cue: Try making the ramyeon.
variations.changed: make it rather than eat it, on the same trial frame

variations.cue: Try adding a little salt.
variations.changed: the trial on a different verb, with jom softening it further

mistake.why: That tells the person to eat. meogeoboseyo offers it instead, and leaves them free to decide they do not like it.

sentences.usage: Recommending a dish without pressing it on anyone.

sentences.cue: Try the new method and see.

words.note: How a thing is done, taken as a whole. With -daero it becomes the way the method says, which is what an instruction sheet asks for.
L1-M4's hada with the trial auxiliary joined on. It is the most useful of these, because almost any noun plus hada can take it.

sentences.trap: haeboseyo IS NOT haseyo WITH A SOFTENER ADDED. haseyo tells someone to do it; haeboseyo says do it and find out. A manager who says haseyo has decided, and one who says haeboseyo has not.
sentences.sound: SAE bang-BEO-beul HAN-beon hae-BO-se-yo. Bangbeop-eul runs together as bang-BEO-beul.

variations.cue: Try this and see.
variations.changed: this one rather than a named method

variations.cue: Try the new method in the order given.
variations.changed: the order of the steps added to the trial

mistake.why: hanbeon invites and haseyo orders, so the two pull against each other. An invitation ends in haeboseyo.

sentences.usage: Suggesting a different way of doing something to a colleague.

sentences.cue: You just have to add a little salt.

words.note: Table salt and cooking salt alike. It is the standard first thing a Korean instruction tells you to add.
Stir two things together. The doubled k of the stem shows up before a vowel ending, so the present is seokkeoyo.

sentences.trap: dwaeyo IS NOT a SECOND VERB. The clause in front of it must end in -(eu)myeon: the pair is one frame meaning that will do it. A finished sentence followed by dwaeyo is not Korean.
sentences.sound: so-GEU-meul JOM neo-EU-myeon DWAE-yo. Sogeum-eul runs together as so-GEU-meul.

variations.display: Sogeum-eul neoeuseyo, geu daeum-e jal seokkeuseyo.
variations.script: 소금을 넣으세요, 그 다음에 잘 섞으세요.
variations.cue: Add the salt, then mix it well.
variations.changed: two instructions in place of the permission

variations.cue: You just have to mix it well.
variations.changed: the step: mixing rather than salting

mistake.why: neoeoyo closes the sentence, and dwaeyo then has nothing to attach to. The clause has to end in -(eu)myeon: neoeumyeon dwaeyo.

sentences.usage: Answering is that all? at the stove or over a recipe.
sentences.mnemonic: -myeon dwaeyo: do that, and you are done.

sentences.cue: You just have to do this in order.

words.note: The everyday spoken word for this thing, said as one token. It is what points at an object when the object has no name yet.

sentences.trap: -daero ATTACHES TO A NOUN AND NOT TO A VERB. sunseo-daero is in that order; a verb wanting the same sense needs a different shape altogether. Written apart, daero would mean nothing at all.
sentences.sound: I-geo-reul SUN-seo-dae-ro HA-myeon DWAE-yo. The -daero rides on sunseo with no break.

variations.cue: Try doing this in order.
variations.changed: a suggestion instead of the permission

variations.cue: You just have to follow the method.
variations.changed: the noun -daero attaches to

mistake.why: sunseo on its own is only the word order, a noun with nothing said about it. -daero is what turns it into in accordance with it.

sentences.usage: Reassuring someone that a form or a machine has no trick to it.
sentences.mnemonic: sunseo is the order, sunseo-daero is following it.

sentences.cue: I study Korean in order to go to Korea.

words.note: L1-M2's gada turned into a noun by -gi. Korean has no infinitive, so a verb that has to sit in front of a postposition is nominalised first.
It follows a -gi stem or a noun and says what the effort is for. It explains rather than instructs, so it reads oddly in front of an order.
The language, built on hanguk plus the -eo that names a tongue. The g is heard across the join, which is why it is written hangugeo.
L1-M4's hada nominalised the same way. It is the most common of these stems, because any noun plus hada can take it.

sentences.trap: KOREAN HAS NO INFINITIVE. English to go is one shape doing two jobs; Korean has neither, and a bare stem in front of wihaeseo is not a word. The stem takes -gi first, every time.
sentences.sound: han-GU-ge GA-gi wi-HAE-seo. Hanguk-e is han-GU-ge, and hangugeo-reul is han-gu-GEO-reul.

variations.cue: I go to the station in order to make a booking.
variations.changed: the purpose built on hada, and a place as the main clause

variations.cue: I make a booking in order to go to Korea.
variations.changed: the purpose kept, and the main clause changed

mistake.why: A bare stem cannot stand in front of wihaeseo. It has to become a noun first, and -gi is what does that: gagi wihaeseo.

sentences.usage: Saying why you are learning something, in an interview or over coffee.
sentences.mnemonic: -gi makes the verb a thing, wihaeseo says what it is for.

sentences.cue: I boil water in order to eat ramyeon.

words.note: L1-M3's meokda nominalised by -gi. The k of the stem stays written, exactly as it does in L1-M3's meokgo.
Both the activity and the dish it produces. With hada it is the verb to cook: yori-reul haeyo.
One verb for use and for write, and the context decides. A pot is sseoyo, and so is a name on a form.

sentences.trap: THE PURPOSE CLAUSE STILL COMES FIRST. English would say I boil water to eat ramyeon; every word of the Korean is in the opposite half of the sentence, and the literal line above shows how far it travels.
sentences.sound: ra-MYEO-neul MEOK-gi wi-HAE-seo. Meokgi keeps its k hard, and kkeuryeoyo is kkeu-RYEO-yo.

variations.cue: I use a pot in order to cook.
variations.changed: the purpose built on hada, and a tool as the main clause

variations.cue: I turn the heat on in order to eat ramyeon.
variations.changed: the step in the main clause

mistake.why: -gi wihaeseo explains why you are doing a thing; it does not tell anyone to do it. An instruction takes -(eu)ryeomyeon in front.

sentences.usage: Explaining your own steps to somebody watching you cook.

If you want to go to the station, go this way.
If you want to make a booking, press this.

You just have to do this in order.

comprehensionPool.cue: First turn the heat on, then boil the water.
